stories.title: Cyclone Murasu: All 70 gates of Prakasam Barrage opened; 71,000 cusecs released into Krishna
stories.summary: The inflows come largely from the Keesara, Munneru and Budameru streams after heavy rain in NTR district
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Heavy rain continues in the Krishna basin under the influence of Cyclone Murasu.
The Water Resources Department (WRD) has suspended water supply to canals and opened all 70 gates of the Prakasam Barrage to send the surplus flow downstream.
The Prakasam Barrage was receiving 71,000 cusecs at 8 a.m. on Wednesday (November 4, 2026), and the entire quantity was being released into the Krishna river towards the Bay of Bengal.
The water level stood at 12 feet.
To facilitate the discharge, 30 gates had been raised by two feet and another 40 by one foot.
WRD officials have stopped releases into the Krishna Eastern, Krishna Western and Guntur canals as a precaution against possible flooding.
The inflows are being fed largely by the Keesara, Munneru and Budameru streams, which drain into the Krishna from the local catchment areas.
Surplus releases from the barrage began on Tuesday night after inflows increased.
The decision to regulate the discharge comes amid reports of exceptionally heavy rainfall in NTR district and forecasts of more rain by the India Meteorological Department.
Officials are keeping a close watch on the river’s inflows and the situation in the upstream catchment areas.
Residents in low-lying settlements along the Krishna riverbanks have been asked to exercise caution and comply with instructions from the authorities.

Edlapadu in Palnadu district received the most rain in the State in the 24 hours ending 8.30 a.m. on Wednesday, 269.45 mm, according to the Andhra Pradesh Directorate of Economics and Statistics (APDES).

stories.title: Cyclone Murasu leaves 2 dead, damages 312 houses in Andhra Pradesh

article_sentences: At least two people were killed in Bapatla district after severe cyclonic storm Murasu battered south coastal Andhra Pradesh on Tuesday, November 3, damaging crops across 52,459 hectares and 312 houses.

Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) Managing Director Prakhar Jain confirmed the deaths and said 12,230 people had been moved to rehabilitation centres across the affected districts.
Guntur, Bapatla and Palnadu were among the worst-affected districts.

According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Murasu crossed the south Andhra Pradesh coast near Ongole in Prakasam district between 3.30 am and 5.30 am on Tuesday with winds of 100-110 kmph.
The cyclone has also triggered heavy to extremely heavy rainfall across coastal Andhra Pradesh, uprooting trees and damaging roads.
Preliminary reports estimate the damage caused by the cyclone at around Rs 344 crore and the government is monitoring 814 minor irrigation tanks, of which 776 have been placed on high alert.
Kothapatnam in Prakasam district recorded 16.4 cm of rainfall between 8.30 am on Monday and 5 am on Tuesday.
Naguluppalapadu in Prakasam received 11.4 cm, followed by Chirala in Bapatla at 10 cm.
Pelluru and Throvagunta in Prakasam recorded 9.3 cm and 9.2 cm, respectively.
Authorities are also monitoring the Budameru rivulet in NTR district, which had triggered floods in Vijayawada in 2024.
Heavy inflows were expected into the rivulet and people living in low-lying areas were shifted to rehabilitation centres.
Residents in parts of Bapatla and NTR districts were moved to shelters overnight amid concerns over heavy rainfall and possible landslides.

stories.headline: SC seeks Centre, EC response on law giving blanket, lifelong immunity to CEC, Election Commissioners
stories.title: SC seeks Centre, EC response on law giving blanket, lifelong immunity to CEC, Election Commissioners
stories.summary: RJD MP Manoj Jha has moved the Supreme Court challenging Section 16 of The Chief Election Commissioner And Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions Of Service And Term Of Office) Act, 2023
reasons: source: event has 3 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: 3 independent source groups -> high confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) sought a response from the Union government on petitions challenging the constitutionality of a specific provision in the Chief Election Commissioner-Election Commissioners’ appointment law which grants them blanket, lifelong immunity from any legal action or criminal prosecution, not only during the official tenure but even after retirement.

A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant issued notice to both the Centre and the Election Commission of India on petitions filed by RJD MP Manoj Jha, represented by Tanya Srivastava and advocate Arun Kumar Agrawal, represented by advocate Neha Rathi, challenging Section 16 of The Chief Election Commissioner And Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions Of Service And Term Of Office) Act, 2023.
The court listed the petitions on December 18.

The petitions said the Section was unconstitutional, went beyond the ambit of powers given to the Election Commission of India (EC) and, significantly, violated the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
“Section 16 of the Act bars jurisdiction of Constitutional courts and interferes with the power of judicial review, held to be a part of the Basic Structure of Constitution,” the petitions submitted.

Ms. Rathi submitted that a plain reading of the provision showed a bar on any court to entertain or continue any civil or criminal proceedings against “any person who is or was a Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner for any act, thing or word, committed, done or spoken by him when, or in the course of acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty or function”.
“A bare perusal of the text [of Section 16] discloses the width of the protection granted in so far as it bars all kinds of prosecution including corruption, forgery and other serious offences.
It provides for lifelong immunity and covers acts that may be outside lawful authority,” Mr. Agrawal’s plea contended.

Section 16 further barred proceedings instituted under defamation law, contempt law and other civil or criminal liabilities for lifetime without distinguishing between mala fide and bona fide acts, all under guise of preventing frivolous complaints against the CEC.
“The object to ensure independence by taking such sweeping measures fails the test of proportionality.
That every person has a right to a remedy and to a fair investigation, and access to justice is a facet of Articles 14 and 21,” the petitioners highlighted.
They said that until the enactment of the 2023 Act, the Parliament had not granted any blanket immunity to Election Commissioners.

article_sentences: Ramaswamy, who minted his billions in the pharmaceutical sector, had challenged Trump for the Republican Party nomination in the 2024 election, but withdrew and endorsed him.
New York: Vivek Ramaswamy, the flamboyant Republican billionaire and fiery acolyte of President Donald Trump, lost the race for governor of Ohio.
He was defeated in Tuesday's election by Democrat Amy Acton, whom Ramaswamy targeted with an ad that even some leaders of his party criticised.
Forbes puts his wealth at about $2.2 billion and his campaign spent about $79 million, most of it from his own funds in the campaign, where he flew around in a private jet.
An ardent supporter of Trump's fiery MAGA (Make America Great Again) ideology, he modelled his campaign after his brash style.
Trump praised his intelligence and rewarded him with an appointment as the co-leader with tech billionaire Elon Musk of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency.
But in a clash of strong personalities, Ramaswamy quit by the time Trump assumed the presidency, opting to run for governor of Ohio.
While he was initially on the upswing, his standing against Acton, a doctor who had been state health director, began to erode alongside Trump's popularity.
Acton had suffered sexual abuse by her stepfather as a child, before a court ordered her removed from her mother and handed her over to her father.
The stepfather, who was charged with sexual abuse, fled the state and remained a fugitive from the law till his death.
Ramaswamy found her mother, who did have contact with Acton for decades and made an ad in which she defended her husband -- Acton's stepfather -- and called her a liar.
While President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance backed the ad, it was seen by others as supportive of a paedophile.

stories.headline: SC upholds states’ power to levy additional sales tax, says case has become academic
stories.title: SC upholds states’ power to levy additional sales tax, says case has become academic
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 04: The Supreme Court on Wednesday held that a 1974 Constitution Bench ruling upholding states’ power to impose additional sales tax or surcharge calculated as a percentage of the existing sales tax continues to hold the field, saying a reference on the issue had become academic. A seven-judge Constitution bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant unanimously held that the legal question referred to it nearly 27 years ago no longer required adjudication, as the statutory provisions under challenge had since been replaced or amended and the Goods and Services Tax (GST) law had come into force. “The question referred to is of no practical significance and now academic. Consequently, the question referred to does not survive for adjudication by a seven-judge Bench, and the reference has to be answered accordingly,” the CJI, who wrote the judgment on behalf of himself and five other judges, said. The bench also comprised Justices K V Viswanathan, S V N Bhatti, Joymalya Bagchi, N V Anjaria, Arun Palli and V Mohana. Justice Viswanathan wrote a separate concurring verdict. While declining to undertake a fresh adjudication on the reference, the court clarified that the five-judge Constitution Bench ruling in S Kodar vs State of Kerala (1974) continued to hold the field. The earlier judgment had upheld additional sales tax, rejecting the argument that such a levy amounted to a tax on the income of dealers. “We have clarified that the case clearly held that an additional tax or surcharge computed as a percentage of the sales tax payable is an enhancement of the rate of sales tax and a tax on the sale or purchase of goods within Entry 54 of List II, as it then stood. That decision continues to hold the field,” the CJI said. The court further held that the question of the legislative competence of state legislatures to impose the surcharge would be governed by the law laid down in S Kodar. The detailed judgment is awaited. The reference arose from a challenge to Section 5A of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, which provided for additional tax at the rate of 10 per cent on dealers with an annual turnover between Rs 10 lakh and Rs 1 crore, and 15 per cent on dealers whose turnover exceeded Rs 1 crore. The appellants questioned whether the state legislature was competent to impose such a levy under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, which empowered states to tax the sale or purchase of goods, or whether it effectively amounted to a tax on income, a subject falling within Parliament’s domain under Entry 82 of List I. The controversy stemmed from differing interpretations in earlier Supreme Court decisions. In S Kodar vs State of Kerala, a five-judge bench had upheld additional sales tax, ruling that a levy calculated with reference to the sales tax payable was an enhancement of the sales tax rate and not a tax on the dealer’s income. During the hearing on September 22, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta submitted that the controversy had largely become academic following the introduction of the GST regime in 2017, with relatively few disputes remaining pending.

stories.headline: Pia Dandiya secures Florida House seat in historic US Congress win
stories.title: Pia Dandiya secures Florida House seat in historic US Congress win
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 4: Pia Dandiya, the daughter of immigrants from Jaipur in Rajasthan, won Florida's 22nd Congressional District, becoming the second Indian American woman elected to the US House of Representatives, after Pramila Jayapal. Dandiya, a Democrat, defeated Republican businessman Casey Askar, according to projections by Decision Desk HQ and CBS News. NBC News showed a 'Projected winner' banner on the race, with Dandiya ahead by about 52 per cent to 48 per cent and about 99 per cent of the expected vote counted. NBC said the race shifted about 14 points towards Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential vote. Born and raised in Palm Beach County, Dandiya grew up in Jupiter, where her parents settled after emigrating from Jaipur in the 1980s. After moving to the US, her father, Dr Rohit Dandiya, continued his medical practice, while her mother, then 40, founded a Montessori school in Jupiter, initially established for Dandiya. Dandiya was raised with strong ties to her Indian heritage, and her parents sent her to India as a child to spend time with her cousins. "Very early on, my parents would send me on a solo trip to India to spend time with my cousins. These trips were life-changing and played a pivotal role in shaping my identity. They helped me understand how different democracies function and gave me a sense of global inequality," she told New India Abroad in an August 2025 interview. After her freshman year at Harvard, she spent a summer teaching English to children aged seven to 17 in the slums of New Delhi with the Asha Cooperative Society. "Teaching those underprivileged kids, I learnt what truly separates people from each other is not their potential, but their circumstances," she said. "I was born and raised in this district by parents who came to this country in pursuit of the American dream, and I've dedicated my career to making sure that dream is within reach for more families," Dandiya said when the Indian American Impact Fund endorsed her in 2025. Dandiya studied government at Harvard and earned a master's in education from Boston University. She taught with Teach For America in Boston and, at 28, became the founding principal of Democracy Prep Endurance High School in Harlem, where about 86 per cent of students were low-income, and every graduate was admitted to college, according to her campaign. "Around 86 per cent of students in my school lived below the poverty. But we promised them a brighter future: if they came to our school, 100 per cent of them would earn admission to college," she told New India Abroad. She was a White House Fellow in 2020, serving on the White House Domestic Policy Council and at the US Department of Education, and later led public-sector initiatives at Apple. Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker appointed her to the state's P-20 Council. This was Dandiya's first run for office. She initially filed to run in the 21st District against Republican Brian Mast, then moved to the open 22nd District after Florida's mid-decade redistricting, and won the Democratic primary on August 18. The district leans Republican by registration, with about 1,85,000 Republicans, 1,46,000 Democrats and 1,50,000 voters with other affiliations, Florida Politics reported. Dandiya campaigned on the cost of living, corruption, healthcare, education and gun safety. "South Floridians are fed up with the rising costs and performative politics coming out of Washington," she told Florida Politics. The race drew heavy money. Through October 14, Dandiya raised about $4.6 million, while Askar raised about $7.4 million, most of it from loans to his own campaign. Askar's self-funding reached about $6.8 million, Federal Election Commission records show. No Going Back PAC, a super PAC funded by MAGA Inc., reported spending about $6.5 million against her by October 24, according to FEC filings. House Majority PAC, the main Democratic super PAC for House races, spent about $7.9 million against Askar. Dandiya won endorsements from the Indian American Impact Fund and Serve America PAC, and from Wellington's Republican mayor, Michael Napoleone. "I've always believed that the person matters more than the party, and Pia has earned my respect and my endorsement," Napoleone said. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg campaigned with her on October 26. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee said on X that she "focused on the issues that matter most to South Florida -- addressing the affordability crisis and making sure that everyone has the opportunity to achieve the American Dream." "Congratulations to @PiaforCongress for winning her election! I am so excited to welcome the third South Asian American woman (along with me and @aishabbwahab) to the House!!!" Indian-American Representative Pramila Jayapal posted on X. Dandiya lives in Palm Beach Gardens with her husband, Navneet Alag, and their son, Sahib. Her win keeps the Indian-American "Samosa Caucus" in the House from shrinking in the new Congress. --IANS

body: NBC News showed a 'Projected winner' banner on the race, with Dandiya ahead by about 52 per cent to 48 per cent and about 99 per cent of the expected vote counted.
NBC said the race shifted about 14 points towards Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential vote.
Born and raised in Palm Beach County, Dandiya grew up in Jupiter, where her parents settled after emigrating from Jaipur in the 1980s.
After moving to the US, her father, Dr Rohit Dandiya, continued his medical practice, while her mother, then 40, founded a Montessori school in Jupiter, initially established for Dandiya.
Dandiya was raised with strong ties to her Indian heritage, and her parents sent her to India as a child to spend time with her cousins.
"Very early on, my parents would send me on a solo trip to India to spend time with my cousins.
These trips were life-changing and played a pivotal role in shaping my identity.
They helped me understand how different democracies function and gave me a sense of global inequality," she told New India Abroad in an August 2025 interview.
After her freshman year at Harvard, she spent a summer teaching English to children aged seven to 17 in the slums of New Delhi with the Asha Cooperative Society.
"Teaching those underprivileged kids, I learnt what truly separates people from each other is not their potential, but their circumstances," she said.

"I was born and raised in this district by parents who came to this country in pursuit of the American dream, and I've dedicated my career to making sure that dream is within reach for more families," Dandiya said when the Indian American Impact Fund endorsed her in 2025.
Dandiya studied government at Harvard and earned a master's in education from Boston University.

She taught with Teach For America in Boston and, at 28, became the founding principal of Democracy Prep Endurance High School in Harlem, where about 86 per cent of students were low-income, and every graduate was admitted to college, according to her campaign.
"Around 86 per cent of students in my school lived below the poverty.
But we promised them a brighter future: if they came to our school, 100 per cent of them would earn admission to college," she told New India Abroad.
She was a White House Fellow in 2020, serving on the White House Domestic Policy Council and at the US Department of Education, and later led public-sector initiatives at Apple.
Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker appointed her to the state's P-20 Council.
This was Dandiya's first run for office.

She initially filed to run in the 21st District against Republican Brian Mast, then moved to the open 22nd District after Florida's mid-decade redistricting, and won the Democratic primary on August 18.
The district leans Republican by registration, with about 1,85,000 Republicans, 1,46,000 Democrats and 1,50,000 voters with other affiliations, Florida Politics reported.
Dandiya campaigned on the cost of living, corruption, healthcare, education and gun safety.
"South Floridians are fed up with the rising costs and performative politics coming out of Washington," she told Florida Politics.
The race drew heavy money.
Through October 14, Dandiya raised about $4.6 million, while Askar raised about $7.4 million, most of it from loans to his own campaign.
Askar's self-funding reached about $6.8 million, Federal Election Commission records show.
Dandiya won endorsements from the Indian American Impact Fund and Serve America PAC, and from Wellington's Republican mayor, Michael Napoleone.
"I've always believed that the person matters more than the party, and Pia has earned my respect and my endorsement," Napoleone said.
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg campaigned with her on October 26.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee said on X that she "focused on the issues that matter most to South Florida -- addressing the affordability crisis and making sure that everyone has the opportunity to achieve the American Dream." "Congratulations to @PiaforCongress for winning her election!

I am so excited to welcome the third South Asian American woman (along with me and @aishabbwahab) to the House!!!" Indian-American Representative Pramila Jayapal posted on X. Dandiya lives in Palm Beach Gardens with her husband, Navneet Alag, and their son, Sahib.
Her win keeps the Indian-American "Samosa Caucus" in the House from shrinking in the new Congress.
--IANS.

stories.title: Supreme Court Asks MP Speaker To Decide Congress Leader's Disqualification Petition Against Nirmala Sapre MLA In 2 Months

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Wednesday directed the Speaker of the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly to decide within two months a pending disqualification petition against Bina MLA Nirmala Sapre under the anti-defection law.

The petition, filed in July 2024 by Congress Leader of Opposition Umang Singhar, alleges that Sapre voluntarily gave up her membership of the Indian National Congress, the party on whose ticket she was elected in the 2023 Assembly polls, and joined the BJP.

Senior Advocate Vivek Tankha, appearing for the petitioner, described it as a “classic case” under the Tenth Schedule, stating that Sapre had left the party and was campaigning with the opposite side, yet the Speaker had not commenced proceedings.

The bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana hearing the matter noted the allegations of voluntary relinquishment of party membership triggering disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
It observed that the petition had remained undecided for over two years.

The Madhya Pradesh High Court had earlier dismissed Singhar's plea seeking a time-bound decision, holding that there was no urgency as proceedings were underway and Sapre had denied resigning from Congress or joining the BJP.
The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's approach on urgency.

It held that even where a court finds no immediate urgency, or where considerable time remains until the Assembly's term expires, petitions under the Tenth Schedule must still be decided expeditiously.
The Court therefore directed the Speaker to decide the disqualification petition within two months.
The Court also cited its precedent in Padi Kaushik Reddy which set a deadline to the Telangana Speaker to decide disqualification petitions.
Sapre, a first-time MLA from Bina in Sagar district, had won the seat on a Congress ticket in 2023.
In May 2024, during the Lok Sabha election campaign, she appeared on a BJP platform in the presence of Chief Minister Mohan Yadav and announced her decision to join the ruling party.

stories.title: Supreme Court Rejects Plea To Rotate SC/ST Reservations Of Assembly & Parliament Seats, Affirms Validity Of S.9(1)(c) Delimitation Act
stories.summary: The Court declined interference, observing that it was a matter of legislative policy.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Court declined interference, observing that it was a matter of legislative policy.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected a plea seeking mandatory rotation of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in State Legislative Assemblies and Parliament, holding that the issue falls within the legislative domain of Parliament and cannot be directed by the courts.

The Court was dealing with a petition challenging Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, 2002, which requires reserved constituencies to be located in areas where the proportion of SC/ST population is comparatively large.
After the Allahabad High Court upheld Section 9(1)(c) and refused to order rotation of reserved seats, the petitioner approached the Supreme Court.

The bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana refused to interfere with the High Court's judgment, observing that it was a matter for the legislature to decide.
The Court allowed the petitioner to file a representation before the elected representatives seeking a change in the law.

The petitioner, Jagdish Singh, an elector of the 191-Kadipur Assembly Constituency in Sultanpur district of Uttar Pradesh, had argued that the seat had remained reserved for SCs for nearly seven decades since its creation.

He contended that the continuous reservation without rotation violated Articles 14, 15 and 19 of the Constitution, diluted the right to vote by compelling voters to choose only from SC candidates, and benefited only a few families rather than the broader community.
He sought a system of rotation similar to that provided for panchayats and municipalities under Articles 243D and 243T.
During the hearing, the bench observed that voters in a multiparty democracy are expected to vote on the basis of political ideology rather than caste or religion.

Justice Bagchi noted that whether concentrating reserved seats in areas with larger SC/ST populations creates caste divisions is a matter for the legislature to examine and does not by itself render the law unconstitutional.

The Court distinguished the constitutional right to vote from any claimed right to contest from a particular constituency, pointing out that general-category candidates can contest from non-reserved seats.

article_sentences: Seven separate prohibitive orders passed by the Delhi.

Police under Section 163 Bharatiya Nagarik Duraksha Sanhita (BNSS) in the national capital show restrictions concerning free movement were imposed way before protests erupted demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.

Six orders issued on August 20 or immediately before or after this date, came a month after the July 20 protests against alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leaks witnessed violence in New Delhi district, the power and commercial heart of the capital city.
One of them imposes prohibitions from September 26 to November 24.
The prohibitive orders are for a maximum period of 60 days, till the latter half of October.
They are ex-parte or without hearing any objections, saying “notice cannot be served individually on all concerned”.
The orders, which are part of an affidavit filed by Delhi.

Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar in the Supreme Court, said “reports have been received indicate that such conditions now exists that unrestricted holding of public meetings, processions/demonstrations, etc, in the area are likely to cause obstruction to traffic, danger to human safety and disturbance of public tranquility”.
The police reasoned in the orders that it was necessary to take “speedy measures” to “prevent danger to human life or safety and disturbance to public tranquility”.

The seven orders comprise the police sub-divisions of Connaught Place, Tughlak Road, Parliament Street, Chanakya Puri — where the Prime Minister’s residence, Rashtrapati Bhavan, foreign embassies, and other vital installations are located — Barakhamba Road, Safdarjung Enclave in south-west Delhi, and Defence Colony.

The orders prohibited activities, including the holding of any public meeting, shouting of slogans, making speeches, picketing or dharnas, assembly of five or more persons, carrying fire arms, banners, placards, lathis, spears, swords, sticks, brickbats, etc.

The affidavit from the police chief came in response to a host of petitions filed by politicians, party leaders, activists, lawyers and private individuals — including CPI(M) state secretary M.A. Baby, Rajya Sabha MP.

stories.title: Supreme Court Asks Centre To Create Special Cell To Monitor Enforcement Of Child Labour Prohibition Act

event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court recently directed the Secretary of the Ministry of Women and Child Development to constitute a special cell to monitor the implementation of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, as amended in 2016, and ensure strict compliance with its provisions.
The Court also directed the Centre to issue instructions to enforcement agencies through the respective Chief Secretaries of States to ensure effective implementation of the law.

A bench comprising Justice SVN Bhatti and Justice NV Anjaria passed the directions while disposing of a writ petition challenging the provisions of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, particularly Section 3, which originally prohibited the employment of children only in specified hazardous occupations.

The petition was disposed of after the Court took note of the 2016 amendment to the Act, which introduced a blanket prohibition on the employment of children below 14 years of age in all occupations and processes, subject to limited exceptions.
The amendment permits children to assist in non-hazardous family enterprises after school hours or during vacations, subject to the statutory conditions.
The bench observed that the prayers raised in the writ petition no longer survived for consideration in view of the legislative changes.
However, it emphasised that the effective implementation of the amended law remained a responsibility of the authorities.
"We take note of the writ prayers, the orders passed by this Court and also the amendment to the parent Act.

We are of the view that the prayer, as made, in the writ petition does not survive for further consideration but what remains to be taken note of is giving complete and full effect to the changes introduced by way of amendment Act No. 35 of 2016.

Keeping in perspective the above brief narrative, we are persuaded not to examine the prayers as made but we take note of the amendment Act No. 35 of 2016 and note that it shall be the responsibility of the respondent(s) to ensure complete and strict compliance of the mandate of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 including the amended provisions.

For the said purpose, with a view to preserving the rights of children/ adolescents, we direct the second respondent to constitute a special cell, continue to monitor the implementation of the provisions of the Act and also issue directions to the enforcing agencies through the respective Chief Secretaries of the State, as amended through the Act No.35 of 2016."

stories.title: Supreme Court 7-Judge Bench Holds Reference On States' Power For Additional Levy On Sales Tax Academic After GST
stories.summary: The Court held that the reference has been rendered infructuous.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Court held that the reference has been rendered infructuous.

A seven-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court, headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, on Wednesday held that a nearly three-decade-old reference on the legislative competence of states to impose additional sales tax or surcharge calculated on existing sales tax has become academic following the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime.

The Constitution Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice KV Viswanathan, Justice SV Bhatti, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice NV Anjaria, and Justice V Mohana was answering a reference arising from Arjun Flour Mills, which concerned Odisha's levy of additional tax at 10% and 15% depending on dealers' annual turnover.

The core constitutional question was whether such a levy fell within the states' taxation powers under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule (as it then stood) or encroached upon Parliament's power to tax income.

Pronouncing the order, CJI Surya Kant said the issue related to the competence of state legislatures to levy a tax on the sale or purchase of goods under the then Entry 54 on the sales tax payable by a dealer rather than directly on his turnover.

The bench examined the entire case law beginning with India Cement, Kodar, the statutory schemes of Odisha and Punjab, and the Punjab Social Security aspect, before turning to the constitutional framework on taxation and the new GST regime that rendered the earlier Acts and statutes redundant.
The Court summarised its conclusions as follows: the reference stemmed from a perceived conflict between Hoechst Pharmaceuticals and India Cement.

India Cement dealt with a cess on royalty in a field covered by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act and did not hold that a levy computed as a percentage of another tax is, for that reason alone, beyond legislative competence.
In principle, such a levy as an increment to an existing tax is to be judged in the same way as that tax.
The premise in India Cement that royalty is a tax has since been overruled by a larger bench in Mineral Area Development Authority.
Consequently, there is no subsisting decision of the Court in conflict with the earlier view.

The Court clarified that an additional tax or surcharge computed as a percentage of the sales tax payable is an enhancement of the rate of sales tax and remains a tax on the sale or purchase of goods within the then Entry 54 of List II.

The core constitutional question was whether such a levy fell within the states' taxation powers under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule (as it then stood) or encroached upon Parliament's power to tax income.

Pronouncing the order, CJI Surya Kant said the issue related to the competence of state legislatures to levy a tax on the sale or purchase of goods under the then Entry 54 on the sales tax payable by a dealer rather than directly on his turnover.

The bench examined the entire case law beginning with India Cement, Kodar, the statutory schemes of Odisha and Punjab, and the Punjab Social Security aspect, before turning to the constitutional framework on taxation and the new GST regime that rendered the earlier Acts and statutes redundant.
The Court summarised its conclusions as follows: the reference stemmed from a perceived conflict between Hoechst Pharmaceuticals and India Cement.

India Cement dealt with a cess on royalty in a field covered by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act and did not hold that a levy computed as a percentage of another tax is, for that reason alone, beyond legislative competence.
In principle, such a levy as an increment to an existing tax is to be judged in the same way as that tax.
The premise in India Cement that royalty is a tax has since been overruled by a larger bench in Mineral Area Development Authority.

stories.headline: US Midterms 2026: Democrats make early gains, Indian-Americans win key races
stories.title: US Midterms 2026: Democrats make early gains, Indian-Americans win key races
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 04: Indian-American Democrats Suhas Subramanyam, Aruna Miller have secured re-election, and Pia Dandiya has clinched victory in the 2026 US midterm elections, marking early successes for candidates from the community as the first results emerged. Subramanyam, 40, was on Tuesday re-elected as US Congressman from Virginia; Miller, 61, retained her position as Maryland’s Lieutenant Governor and Dandiya, 39, won Florida’s 22nd congressional district. Meanwhile, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy was trailing in Ohio’s governor’s race. Americans voted in the most consequential midterm elections, which early surveys predicted as a rebuke to President Donald Trump, signalling a mood for change. Other Indian-American candidates are awaiting their results; vote counting was still underway. Republican Shelley Capito from West Virginia and Democrat Wesley Bell in Missouri's 1st Congressional District have won re-election. Democrats flipped a Senate seat in North Carolina and won races in Georgia and New Hampshire on Tuesday. Former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper won against Republican Michael Whatley. Over 210 million Americans were eligible to vote in the elections, which began at 6.00 am eastern time on Tuesday for 435 seats of the US House of Representatives, 37 seats of the US Senate, 36 posts of state governors and a slew of local public offices. According to some preliminary national results of CNN’s Voter Poll, voters were broadly unhappy with the state of the nation, the condition of the economy and Trump’s job performance. Trump was in his White House office throughout the day with his advisors as Americans lined up to vote at polling booths across the country. On Tuesday afternoon, he shared endorsements for Republican candidates in a series of posts on X. Speaking to staffers and volunteers at a phone bank in Washington, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the Democrats were on the “brink of dramatic change” and on the “brink” of taking back the House. “We’re going to deliver a Congress that actually puts the American people first,” he said. A Fox News voters’ survey found that the most important issue facing the country is the economy, followed closely by the state of democracy. At the White House, Trump was watching the pre-election results coverage on Fox News but complained about a liberal commentator on the television channel. “Watching the Pre-Election Results on Fox News, but I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me. Have to go somewhere else until that LOSER is off the air — I’ll be back later,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. Throughout the day, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and Interior Secretary Doug Burgham and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin spoke to reporters about the achievements of the Trump administration. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was seen entering the West Wing of the White House and indicated that he would not like to speak. In a post on X, Vice President J D Vance sought to remind voters about the Trump administration's effort to cut taxes over the past year and a half. “We ended taxes on overtime. We ended taxes on tips. We ended taxes on Social Security,” Vance wrote on the social media platform. On polling day, Trump sprung a surprise by announcing that the US will stop providing Israel USD 4 billion in aid from next year, which Democrat Ro Khanna described as a desperate attempt to stave off a Blue tsunami. The elections will decide whether President Trump's Republican Party retains control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers of the US Congress, or, as opinion polls are predicting, the Democratic Party wrests control of at least the House if not the Senate, also in the final two years of Trump's second term in office. On the eve of the elections, the US launched limited strikes on Iran's Qesham island in the Hormuz Strait. Officials said that the strikes were in response to Iran firing at a US aircraft. Democrat Nithya Raman, who was born in Kerala, is locked in a keen contest with her former boss Karen Bass for the post of Mayor of Los Angeles, the US's second-largest city. Indian-American lawmakers Ro Khanna, Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal are seeking re-election to the US House of Representatives, while fellow Democrat Amish Shah is in the fray in competitive races to make their debut as Congresspersons. If the pre-poll forecasts come true and Democrats take control of the US Congress, it will allow for deeper Congressional scrutiny and checks of Trump's actions, which will severely limit his ability to push his agenda. He will, however, retain the power to govern through executive orders, which will be valid for two years. Trump acknowledged the possibility of his wings being clipped but indicated that he will not allow Congress to slow him down. "I guess I'll become Mr Veto," Trump told the New York Post's Pod Force One podcast in response to a question on Republicans losing control of both Houses of the US Congress, referring to the presidential power to veto actions by Congress. The Democrats are hoping to flip seven Senate seats -- Michigan, Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Texas, Iowa and Alaska -- in their bid to gain a majority in the 100-member House. Each of the 50 states in the United States is represented by two Senators who sit in the Congress for a six-year term. But the Senators are divided into three lots, and their terms are staggered so that elections are held every two years. The House members are elected for a two-year term. Republicans enjoy a majority in both chambers of Congress, but by thin margins. In the House of Representatives, Speaker Mike Johnson has 218 Republicans and one independent, Kevin Kiley of California, against 214 Democrats, with two seats vacant. The Senate is split 53-47 in favour of the Republicans. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to wrest control of the chamber. Of the 35 Senate seats on the ballot, 22 are held by Republicans.
